title: Saturday is last day of early voting — and last chance to register to vote in NC - WRAL

 Saturday is last day of early voting — and last chance to register to vote in NC
 Voters can cast their ballots at any early voting location in the county where they’re registered to vote before 3 p.m. on Saturday. And for anyone who isn’t registered to vote, or needs to update their information, Saturday is the last chance.

 By WRAL News staff
 Early voting in North Carolina ends at 3 p.m. Saturday, bringing with it the last chance for people to cast a ballot, register to vote or update their voter information if needed before Election Day.
 The final day of early voting is typically among the busiest, so lines might be long in some places. 
 Other WRAL Top Stories
 North Carolinians this year have already proven they’re excited about casting their ballot: The turnout as of Thursday had already broken the state record for most ballots cast during early voting in a midterm election. Already about one-third of eligible North Carolina voters have cast a ballot. 
 The high turnout has largely been driven by Democratic and unaffiliated voters, who combined have cast nearly 75% of the ballots as of Thursday, according to the most up-to-date state data .
 Voters can find their local sites online at the state or county election board websites. Voters can cast their ballots at any early voting location in the county where they’re registered to vote. A total of 370 early voting sites are open statewide.
 Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Polls on that day will be open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. Voters are assigned precincts for Election Day voting.
 Updating your registration in early voting
 State law allows people to register to vote — and then immediately cast a ballot — during early voting, but not on Election Day, which is Tuesday.
 The only exception is for people who only become eligible to vote in those few days between the end of early voting and Election Day, such as newly naturalized citizens or felons who complete their sentences and regain their rights.
 But for anyone else — those who need to register for the first time, or those who need to update their registration — Saturday is the last chance this election cycle.
 People who need to update their name or address can do so at early voting sites on Saturday, as long as they bring documents to help prove the change. An updated driver’s license would help, especially since state law requires photo identification to vote anyway, but there are other options .
 What's on my ballot?
 Voters will decide races for Congress, the state legislature, courts and local offices, along with ballot questions that vary by location. To see a sample ballot with your specific candidates and ballot questions, use the state's voter lookup tool .
 What if I need assistance?
 Curbside voting is available for voters who cannot enter a polling place without physical assistance because of age or disability. Voters may also request help from poll workers or bring an eligible person to assist them.
 Can I bring my phone?
 Yes, to look up candidate information. But taking a photo of your completed ballot is illegal , and voters cannot use their phones to communicate with others while inside the voting booth.
 What about voting by mail?
 Voters who already received an absentee ballot can return it to an election official at an early voting location in their county, to their county elections board or by mail. You can track its progress through the mail using the state's BallotTrax app .
 And those who change their minds don't have to vote by mail even if they requested a mail-in ballot. They can ask elections officials to cancel it and vote in person instead, as long as they don't vote twice. Or they can fill out the mail-in ballot and hand-deliver it, either to an early voting poll place before the end of early voting Saturday at 3 p.m., or after that, by delivering it to their county elections board office on Monday or Tuesday — before polls close at at 7:30 p.m.
 A relatively new state law eliminated the post-election grace period for ballots to still be counted if they arrived a few days late, as long as they were postmarked on or before Election Day. Now, any ballots that arrive after polls close at 7:30 p.m. Tuesday will be thrown out, no matter when they were put in the mail.
